Reproducing Netflix EDA: From R to Python

A reproduction and extension of Kanigara (2021)

Authors

Yuhan Wen

Linh Tran

Yuezhang Chen

Published

June 3, 2026

1. Introduction

1.1 Original Study

This report reproduces the Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) conducted by Evan Kanigara in R, available at: github.com/evankanigara/Netflix-Movies-and-TV-Show-EDA.

The original study uses the Netflix Movies and TV Shows dataset (Shivam Bansal, Kaggle) and analyses content trends across Movies and TV Shows available on Netflix up to 2021.

1.2 Our Approach

We follow the project structure described in Kanigara (2021) and:

  1. Translate all R code to Python using a class-based package (netflix_analysis)
  2. Reproduce each key finding from the original analysis
  3. Document any differences encountered during reproduction
  4. Extend the analysis with additional questions on duration, ratings, content portfolio structure, and growth forecasting

1.3 Research Questions

Reproduced from original study:

  • RQ1: How has the volume of content added to Netflix changed annually?
  • RQ2: Is Netflix shifting from Movies to TV Shows?
  • RQ3: Which countries contribute the most titles?
  • RQ4: What genres dominate the platform?

Our extensions:

  • RQ5: How has average movie duration changed over the years?
  • RQ6: What is the distribution of content ratings?
  • RQ7: How diversified is Netflix’s catalogue by country and genre?
  • RQ8: What does a simple trend forecast suggest about future content additions?

2.1 Data Cleaning

The original R study handled missing values as follows:

  • director: filled with "Unknown"
  • cast: filled with "Unknown"
  • country: filled with "Unknown" (we follow the same approach)
  • date_added: dropped rows with missing dates (R used na.omit)

Differences encountered: R’s lubridate parses dates more flexibly than Python’s pd.to_datetime. We added .str.strip() to handle leading whitespace in the original CSV, which caused 3 rows to fail parsing silently in R.

Code 
cleaner = NetflixDataCleaner(raw_df)
clean_df = cleaner.clean()
explorer = NetflixExplorer(clean_df)
plotter  = NetflixPlotter("output/figures")

print(f"Clean dataset: {len(clean_df):,} rows")
print(f"Dropped: {info['rows'] - len(clean_df):,} rows")
Clean dataset: 8,794 rows
Dropped: 13 rows

3. RQ1 — Yearly Content Additions

Code 
yearly = explorer.yearly_additions()
plotter.plot_yearly_additions(yearly)
Saved: output/figures/yearly_additions.png

Reproduction result: ✅ Successfully reproduced.

The original R chart (using ggplot2) and our Python chart (using matplotlib) show the same pattern: steady growth from 2015, peaking in 2019, followed by a notable decline in 2020–2021. The visual style differs (R uses a stacked bar, we use a stacked area) but the underlying data is identical.

The original study reported Movies at ~70% and TV Shows at ~30%. Our Python output matches these proportions exactly (Movies: 6,131 / TV Shows: 2,676, after cleaning). No discrepancies found.

5. RQ3 — Top Contributing Countries

Code 
countries = explorer.top_countries()
print(countries)
plotter.plot_top_countries(countries)
country
United States     3680
India             1046
United Kingdom     803
Canada             445
France             393
Japan              317
Spain              232
South Korea        231
Germany            226
Mexico             169
Name: count, dtype: int64
Saved: output/figures/top_countries.png

Reproduction result: ⚠️ Minor difference.

The original R code takes only the first listed country per title (str_split(country, ", ")[[1]][1]). Our implementation explodes all countries (a title with 3 co-producing countries is counted for each). This leads to slightly higher absolute counts in our version, though the ranking (USA → India → UK) is preserved. We consider this an improvement, as the original approach under-counts co-productions.

7. RQ5 — Movie Duration Trend (Extension)

Code 
duration = explorer.movie_duration_trend()
plotter.plot_movie_duration_trend(duration)
Saved: output/figures/movie_duration_trend.png

This analysis was not present in the original study. We find that average movie duration has remained relatively stable at around 90–100 minutes since 1990, with a slight upward trend in the 2000s followed by a mild decrease post-2015.

8. RQ6 — Rating Distribution (Extension)

Code 
ratings = explorer.rating_distribution()
plotter.plot_rating_distribution(ratings)
Saved: output/figures/rating_distribution.png

The majority of Netflix content is rated TV-MA or TV-14, targeting adult and teenage audiences respectively. This was not analysed in the original study.

9. RQ7 — Content Portfolio Analysis (Extension)

Code 
from netflix_analysis.analysis import ContentPortfolioAnalyser

portfolio = ContentPortfolioAnalyser(clean_df)
country_allocation = portfolio.country_allocation()
genre_allocation = portfolio.genre_allocation()
hhi = portfolio.herfindahl_index()
us_dependency = portfolio.us_dependency()

plotter.plot_country_allocation(country_allocation)
plotter.plot_genre_allocation(genre_allocation)
plotter.plot_hhi(hhi)
plotter.plot_us_dependency(us_dependency)
Saved: output/figures/country_allocation.png
Saved: output/figures/genre_allocation.png
Saved: output/figures/country_hhi.png
Saved: output/figures/us_dependency.png

This extension treats the Netflix catalogue as a content portfolio. Countries and genres are interpreted as allocation categories, similar to asset classes in a financial portfolio. This helps us discuss whether Netflix depends too strongly on a small number of markets or whether the catalogue is becoming more diversified.

We also calculate the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI), a concentration measure often used in economics and finance. A higher HHI means the catalogue is more concentrated in a few countries, while a lower HHI indicates better diversification.

10. RQ8 — Growth Forecasting (Extension)

Code 
from netflix_analysis.analysis import ContentGrowthForecaster

forecaster = ContentGrowthForecaster(clean_df)
forecast = forecaster.linear_forecast(forecast_years=3)
r2 = forecaster.r_squared()
moving_average = forecaster.moving_average()
growth = forecaster.growth_rate()

plotter.plot_growth_forecast(forecast, r2)
plotter.plot_moving_average(moving_average)
plotter.plot_yoy_growth(growth)
Saved: output/figures/growth_forecast.png
Saved: output/figures/moving_average.png
Saved: output/figures/yoy_growth.png

We extend the original EDA with a simple growth forecasting exercise. A linear trend model is fitted to yearly Netflix content additions from 2015 to 2021, and the model is used to create a short three-year forecast.

This should not be interpreted as a strong predictive model. Instead, it is a small reproducible extension showing how the cleaned dataset can support additional analysis. The moving average and year-over-year growth charts help describe the trend more smoothly.

Key Challenges

1. Date parsing: the date_added column has inconsistent whitespace not handled in the original R code. Python’s stricter parser required explicit .str.strip().

2. Country counting: the original R analysis only counted the first listed country per title, potentially under-representing co-productions. Our approach explodes the list, giving a more accurate picture.

3. Package ecosystem: R’s ggplot2 + dplyr pipeline required careful translation to pandas + matplotlib. The logic is equivalent but the syntax differs significantly.

12. Reproducibility

This project is fully reproducible via Docker:

docker pull yuhan023/netflix-analysis:latest
docker run --rm \
  -v $(pwd)/data:/app/data \
  -v $(pwd)/output:/app/output \
  yuhan023/netflix-analysis:latest

Or using Make:

make install && make run

Full source code: github.com/ywen2-dot/the-project-of-reproducible-research
